transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
The U.N.'s top court, the International Court of Justice in The Hague, has ruled that Myanmar
committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority.
The ruling is a landmark judgment with far-reaching implications for international justice.
Anna Holigan has more from The Hague.
This is an historic ruling.
The first time the ICJ has found a state responsible for genocide.
The court concluded that around 10,000 Rohingya were killed during a 2017 operation to move
them.
The court judge Yuji Iwasawa said the contacts surrounding the military campaign to clear
the group from the area had created an atmosphere conducive to the violence.
This included anti-Rahindja hate speech portraying the minority as subhuman and a violent threat.
The judge also said brutal sexual violence was intended to physically and mentally impair
people's willingness and ability to have children and to cause trauma and stigma.
He said the killing of babies in the burning down of villages could not be considered a
necessary part of military operations.
The ruling is likely to be closely studied as a precedent for other cases, including
in Gaza, where Israel denies genocide.
For NPR News, I'm Anna Holigan in The Hague.
President Trump has concluded his trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping
and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Chinese and Russian officials have released a readout of the meeting.
They say they agree the International Criminal Court must not abuse their jurisdiction.
They also want to reform the UN.
The US has not released its readout of the conversation.
During the trilateral meeting, Trump stressed his view of global denuclearization.
The Chinese and Russian readouts also agreed on the need to reduce nuclear risks.
European leaders are gathering in Berlin with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Whitkoff.
They're discussing how to broker a peace deal between Ukraine and Russia.
As Esme Nicholson reports, the meeting will also address how to safeguard any potential
ceasefire.
As President Trump's meeting with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin comes
to an end, German Chancellor Friedrich Metz is hosting Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky and
the Coalition of the Willing Allies in Berlin.
The meeting, which includes France's Emmanuel Macron and the United Kingdom's Andy Burnham
as well as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Whitkoff, is another attempt to end nearly
five years of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Writing on X, Kushner stressed that Washington's priority is to work towards a unified position
on the key elements of a lasting peace.
He added that he and Whitkoff are eager to explore how the coalition of the willing can
reduce the risk of future conflict.
For NPR News, I'm Esme Nicholson in Berlin.
On Wall Street, in pre-market trading, Dow futures are up 300 points.
This is NPR.
Big tech company Anthropic has put nearly one billion shares on the market.
Each share is priced at $83 each.
The initial public offering brings in more than $81 billion, and it eclipses the IPO
earlier this year from Elon Musk's SpaceX, that garnered $75 billion.
Today, Anthropic will begin trading on the tech-heavy NASDAQ index.
That is up more than 500 points, or about 2 percent.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.
It's the final week of negotiations at the COP31 UN climate talks.
For being held in Antalya, Turkey, NPR's Rachel Waldholz reports countries are warning
there's a possibility the negotiations could fail.
Delegates from nearly 200 countries are in the last days of annual talks on how to cut
climate pollution and provide funding for developing countries.
Panama Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro told reporters the COP31 negotiations are
not moving fast enough to help countries like his.
Let's call a spade a spade.
Our COPs have become an exercise in hypocrisy and futility.
Talks are set to end Friday, though they could drag into the weekend.
The U.S. is one of the few countries not participating.
Rachel Waldholz, NPR News, Antalya.
Officials with the Cincinnati Zoo say their beloved hippo, Fiona, has swallowed a hat.
They say that Fiona cannot have surgery to retrieve it, and she will need to allow nature
to take its course.
To assist this process, zookeepers are having Fiona stand on a vibrating plate.
This is NPR.

topics.text: ICJ rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims in landmark judgment
Trump concludes trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Putin; readouts diverge on nuclear risk
European leaders meet in Berlin with US envoys Kushner and Witkoff on Ukraine peace deal
Anthropic IPO raises over $81 billion, eclipsing SpaceX's earlier listing
COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey face possible failure in final days
Cincinnati Zoo says hippo Fiona swallowed a hat; surgery ruled out
